abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial dysfunction alters cellular metabolism, increases tissue oxidative stress, and may be principal to the dysregulated signaling and function of CD4 + T lymphocytes in the elderly. In this proof of principle study, it is investigated whether the transfer of functional mitochondria into CD4 + T cells that are isolated from old mice (aged CD4 + T cells), can abrogate aging‐associated mitochondrial dysfunction, and improve the aged CD4 + T cell functionality. The results show that the delivery of exogenous mitochondria to aged non‐activated CD4 + T cells led to significant mitochondrial proteome alterations highlighted by improved aerobic metabolism and decreased cellular mitoROS. Additionally, mito‐transferred aged CD4 + T cells showed improvements in activation‐induced TCR‐signaling kinetics displaying markers of activation (CD25), increased IL‐2 production, enhanced proliferation ex vivo. Importantly, immune deficient mouse models (RAG‐KO) showed that adoptive transfer of mito‐transferred naive aged CD4 + T cells, protected recipient mice from influenza A and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections. These findings support mitochondria as targets of therapeutic intervention in aging.

Introduction

Discussion
Mitochondria are indispensable for proper T cell homeostasis,
[
8
,
11
,
13
,
122
,
123
]
and aging‐associated decline in adaptive immunity is linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance.
[
112
,
122
,
124
,
125
,
126
]
The restoration of redox balance through the reconstitution of mitochondrial fitness (mito‐transfer) in lymphocytes from old mice and older humans has not been thoroughly examined. Our results support our hypothesis that restoration via mito‐transfer would improve immunological CD4
+
T cell functions. We also show that by simply adjusting the ratio of donor mitochondria to recipient CD4
+
T cells per mito‐transfer, the efficiency of mitochondrial transfer to CD4
+
T cells improved from 10 to 100%.
In our experiments using CD4
+
T cells from old mice, mito‐transfer altered the basal levels of mitoROS and a majority of antioxidant proteins, shifting cells towards lower basal levels of intracellular ROS. Importantly, in this study, CD4
+
T cells were defined as “old” based on their isolation from mice that were 18 months or older. This mouse age range is equivalent to ∼ 65 year old individuals. Indeed, primary CD4
+
T cells isolated from old mice (≥ 18‐months) are commonly used in ageing studies, and are characterized by their significant decline in cellular activation, proliferation and cytokine production in comparison to CD4
+
T cells isolated from young (2 to 4 month old) mice.
[
113
,
114
,
127
,
128
]
Proteomic analysis (IPA and GO term enrichment) of mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells from old mice showed that the most upregulated cellular pathways and processes were related to mitochondrial remodeling and Ox‐Phos. Visually, this was corroborated by qualitative EM images, where the cristae ultrastructure of mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells was much denser than non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells. This is in accordance with studies showing that increased mitochondrial cristae density does not always reflect an overall increase in mitochondrial mass, but increased cristae density correlates with elevated oxygen consumption.
[
129
]
Moreover, extracellular flux analysis of mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells showed enhanced aerobic respiration, which is supported by our proteomic data. Our data on mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number hint that mito‐transfer perhaps transiently increased mitochondrial mass before or during the cellular reprogramming process. At a minimum, the increased mitochondrial activity can be attributed to the increased expression of proteins related to ETC. This also is likely the reason behind the concurrent rise in glycolysis in mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells, as the amount of acetyl‐CoA needed for the TCA cycle significantly increased. Acetyl‐CoA is primarily generated either through β‐oxidation of intracellular fatty acids or glycolysis.
[
130
]
We did not assess the preferential utilization of lipids in this study, and the medium preparation used to perform the metabolic analysis did not contain a significant amount of lipids. In line with Le Chatelier's principles of substrate equilibrium, it can be argued that after mito‐transfer, CD4
+
T cells from old mice upregulated glycolysis to compensate for lagging intracellular levels of acetyl‐CoA. Additionally, the ATP production rate of CD4
+
T cells isolated from old mice rose by 40% in comparison to non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells. Primary information regarding T cell metabolism in the context of aging is still sparse.
[
131
]
As of now, it seems the impact of mito‐transfer on the metabolism of CD4
+
T cells differs from the Warburg phenomenon, as there was no bias towards glycolysis, and mito‐transfer decreased mitoROS in the CD4
+
T cells from old mice. Moreover, these data collectively suggest that the mitochondrial cristae of CD4
+
T cells restructured after mito‐transfer, favoring increased cristae density per mitochondria rather than an increase in mitochondrial mass.
Increased cristae density would also explain why the level of mitoROS was significantly higher than that of non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells after mito‐transferred CD4
+
from old mice were activated with PMA/IONO. We also noted that the switch from Ox‐Phos to aerobic glycolysis in mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells was much faster than that of non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells from old mice. Beyond the observed impact on ROS and metabolism, there were other improved T cell functions. We identified significant improvements in TCR‐signaling kinetics, expression of a T cell activation marker (CD25), cytokine production, and an increase in activation‐induced proliferation. Compared to non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells, the proportion of activated T cells expressing CD25
+
and CD69
+
doubled after mito‐transfer and 24 h of activating stimulus. We also noted a concomitant doubling of CD4
+
T cells producing IL‐2, which correlated with increased cell proliferation and contributed to the alteration of cytokine profiles.
The IL‐2 signaling pathway is immunomodulatory,
[
115
,
132
,
133
]
and while CD4
+
T cells, CD8
+
T cells, NK cells, NK T cells, and dendritic cells are all capable of secreting IL‐2, activated CD4
+
T cells are its largest producer.
[
58
,
132
,
134
]
Previous research has shown that CD4
+
T cells from elderly humans and mice produce insufficient amounts of IL‐2, as well as insufficiently express the high‐affinity IL‐2 receptor IL‐2Rα (CD25) necessary for signal transduction.
[
62
,
63
]
Moreover, the current consensus is that aging‐associated defects in IL‐2 signaling can dynamically shift the architecture of adaptive immune responses or even promote T cell anergy.
[
3
,
62
,
64
]
The underlying mechanics regarding blunted IL‐2 production and related signaling in the elderly are still unclear.
[
3
,
64
,
65
]
Intracellular IL‐2 signaling transduction occurs through the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activation of transcription factor (JAK/STAT), phosphoinositide‐3‐kinase (PI3K), and mitogen‐activated kinase (MAPK) pathways, all of which are sensitive to oxidative modifications.
[
66
,
67
]
Previous studies have also characterized the role of redox equilibrium in maintaining proper lymphocyte function, and mitoROS, specifically H
2
O
2
, modulates IL‐2 expression in T cells.
[
13
,
68
]
Supplementation with the antioxidant vitamin E improved the ability of T cells from the elderly to produce IL‐2 and proliferate.
[
69
]
However, maintaining the intracellular redox balance is delicate,
[
9
,
18
,
19
]
and excess antioxidants can hinder proper T cell activation and cytokine production as others have described.
[
70
,
71
]
Our in vivo IAV and
M.tb
infection outcomes highlight the potential of mito‐transfer as an immune‐booster in the elderly. We demonstrated that mito‐transfer can enhance control of viral and non‐viral pathogen infections in vivo, and the enhanced protection is likely related to the preferential generation of antigen‐specific effector memory CD4
+
T cells. As little as 2.0×10
6
naïve mito‐transferred CD4
+
T cells from old mice were capable of differentiating into either IAV or
M.tb
specific effector CD4
+
T cells that had a physiological impact on IAV‐induced morbidity and mortality and on
M.tb
burden. This study could not fully delineate whether antigen‐specific effector CD4
+
T cell quality (antigen‐specific) and or quantity (proliferative capacity) was preferentially enhanced by mito‐transfer. Based on our collective data, we hypothesize that both parameters (i.e., antigen specificity and proliferative capacity) might improve in vivo, and consider that improved disease outcomes should be achievable with an increase in the quantity of mito‐transferred naïve T cells injected into mice.
The capacity to upscale the process of mito‐transfer from in vitro/ex vivo towards in vivo models is likely limited by available techniques to perform mito‐transfer and the number of viable mitochondria or mtDNA needed to revert a specific mitochondrial metabolic abnormality in an organism.
[
72
,
73
]
Mitochondrial encapsulation or injections can facilitate in vivo studies
[
74
,
75
]
and Chang et al. showed that cell‐penetrating peptide (pep‐1) mediated delivery of healthy mitochondria to MCF‐7 breast cancer cells reversed Warburg metabolism, decreased oxidative stress, and increased cancer cell susceptibility to chemotherapeutics.
[
74
]
Zhang et al.,
[
76
]
Jiang et al.,
[
42
]
and Court et. al.
[
78
]
also independently reported on the ability of mito‐transfer to rescue dysfunction in distinct disease models. Specifically, Zhang's research focused on rescuing anthracycline‐induced (Doxorubicin) cardiomyopathy using mitochondria from induced pluripotent stem cell‐derived mesenchymal stem cells (iPSC‐MSCs).
[
76
]
Coculture experiments with iPSC‐MSC and neonatal cardiomyocytes (NCM) exposed to Doxorubicin revealed that iPSC‐MSC donated mitochondria to damaged NCM via tunneling nanotubes (TNT). Although the transfer efficiency between iPSC‐MSC and NCM was reported at ∼35%, the mito‐transfer significantly improved aerobic metabolism in recipient NCM and reduced Dox‐induced oxidative stress, necrosis, and apoptosis, as well as protected against Dox‐induced cardiomyopathy in mice.
[
76
]
Similar improvements were reported by Jiang et al. in their study that assessed mito‐transfer from MSC to corneal epithelial cells (CECs).
[
77
]
Although mito‐transfer between healthy MSC and ECs occurred organically, increased damage to CEC (via rotenone) substantially increased TNT‐mediated mito‐transfer efficiency from 20% to 60%. Improved Ox‐Phos in rotenone‐exposed CEC after mito‐transfer from MSC was also reported, and mito‐transfer of MSC mitochondria to sodium hydroxide exposed rabbit corneas improved healing in vivo.
[
77
]
Court et al. reported on mito‐transfer from MSC to human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), especially CD4
+
T cells.
[
78
]
Using a combination of fluorescent labeling and co‐culture techniques, they found that MSCs rapidly and dose‐dependently transferred mitochondria to various PBMC subsets, especially CD4+ T‐helper cells. The highest mito‐transfer efficiency achieved by Court et al. was ∼40%. Authors also showed through artificial mito‐transfer, “mitoception”, that CD3+ T cells could accept functional mitochondria from MSCs, leading to changes in their metabolic activity and gene expression.
[
78
]
Notably, this mitochondrial transfer method, which involved co‐incubation of isolated mitochondria, induced differentiation of T cells into regulatory T cells (Tregs) with suppressive capabilities. RNA sequencing revealed differential gene expression associated with T‐cell activation and regulation. In murine models, the therapeutic potential of this mitochondrial transfer was evident, with improved outcomes in mouse models of graft‐versus‐host disease (GVHD).
[
78
]
Several distinctions can be made between our work, and the ones summarized above. These studies predominantly employed MSCs as their mitochondrial source and cell‐to‐cell contact (tunneling nanotubes (TNTs)) and extracellular engulfment for mito‐transfer. First, we sourced our mitochondria from mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) rather than MSCs. Secondly, instead of relying on “natural” transfer mechanisms, we employed centrifugation to deliver mitochondria to target cells. Lastly, our mito‐transfer efficiency reached 100%, surpassing the efficiencies reported in these studies, which were ∼35% for cardiomyocytes, ∼60% for corneal cells and ∼40% for T cells. Further comparisons and distinctions could be made between our work and the work by Court et al., specifically relating to T cell metabolism and T cell activation.
[
78
]
Indeed, in Court et al., when compared to non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells, the basal respiration of CD4
+
T cells did not change after mito‐transfer. However, increases in the maximum, spare respiratory capacity, and basal glycolysis were observed.
[
78
]
In our study, when compared to non‐manipulated CD4
+
T cells from old mice, mito‐transfer significantly increased both basal Ox‐Phos and glycolysis in CD4
+
T cells from old mice. These differences could be due to several factors, including the amount of mitochondria transferred and the age of T cells, where in our model, mito‐transfer was done in old T cells, while Court et al. examined mito‐transfer in T cells and PBMCs from healthy donors. Nevertheless, in both works done by Court et al. and andour team, improved T cell function was observed. Court et al. reported upregulation in critical transcripts related to T‐cell activation (e.g., IL2RA‐CD25) after mito‐transfer in CD4
+
T cells,
[
78
]
while we demonstrated that mito‐transfer significantly improved the TCR signalosome and phosphorylation kinetics in CD4+ T cells from old mice and increased in IL‐2 expression and other cytokines.
Our work adds to rapidly growing research evaluating the therapeutic potential of mito‐transfer. Mito‐transfer is an especially promising avenue for the immunological landscape, partly because it is plausibly easy to isolate and re‐insert autologous and allogeneic lymphocytes/leukocytes in a clinic or lab setting. This could have a transformative impact on aging‐associated immune dysregulations and on immune‐based dysregulations that generally involve mitochondrial dysfunction. For example, work by Vaena et al. showed that anti‐tumor T cells from aged individuals succumb to ceramide accumulation‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction and this consequently inhibits anti‐tumor T cell responses.
[
79
]
It would be interesting to assess whether mito‐transferred anti‐tumor CD8
+
T cells from aged mice and elderly can mitigate ceramide‐induce mito‐dysfunction and promote anti‐tumor activity. Guo et al. and team also demonstrated that mitochondrial reprogramming through upregulation of mitochondrial pyruvate carrier was essential to restoring the functionality of exhausted CD8
+
T cells, and this improved their anti‐tumor capacities.
[
80
]
Undoubtedly, future studies will need to investigate the full potential of mito‐transfer on anti‐tumor immunity.
In conclusion, under our experimental conditions, mito‐transfer decreased mitochondrial dysfunction, improved T cell activation, cytokine production, and proliferation of CD4
+
T cells from old mice. Importantly, mito‐transfer had a physiological impact on IAV‐induced morbidity and mortality, and on
M.tb
burden in vivo. In addition to mitoROS mediated redox signaling,

,

,

]
calcium mobilization and buffering in coordination with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER),
[
8
,
9
,
25
,
83
]
cytochrome c mediated apoptosis,
[
55
,
84
,
85
,
119
,
120
]
NAD

[
86

]
as well as protein transport and degradation,

are all interdependent on proper mitochondrial form and function. We suspect that the impact of mito‐transfer on other aspects of T cell function was also improved. More in‐depth mechanistic studies outside the scope of this current study are warranted to elucidate the specific means by which mito‐transfer altered the pathways in CD4
